---
title: "Benchmarks"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)

# The results are CSV files written by `bench/02-run-benchmarks.R`.
find_root <- function(dir = getwd()) {
  while (!file.exists(file.path(dir, "DESCRIPTION"))) {
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) {
      stop("Cannot find the package root.")
    }
    dir <- parent
  }
  dir
}
results_dir <- file.path(find_root(), "bench", "results")
read_result <- function(name) {
  utils::read.csv(
    file.path(results_dir, paste0(name, ".csv")),
    encoding = "UTF-8",
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

cases <- read_result("cases")
build <- read_result("build")
correctness <- read_result("correctness")
comparison <- read_result("comparison")
api <- read_result("api")
env <- read_result("environment")
env <- stats::setNames(env$value, env$key)

method_labels <- c(
  ahocorasick = "ahocorasick",
  polars = "polars",
  polars_native = "polars (native)",
  AhoCorasickTrie = "AhoCorasickTrie",
  base = "base R",
  stringr = "stringr"
)

# Two significant digits below 10, so that small ratios such as 0.05 stay
# visible, and one decimal above.
fmt_ratio <- function(x) {
  trimws(ifelse(
    x < 10,
    formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, flag = "#"),
    formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
  ))
}

fmt_ms <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    is.na(x),
    "–",
    trimws(formatC(signif(x, 3), format = "fg", digits = 3, big.mark = ","))
  )
}

# One row per case, one column per method: the median time and how many times
# slower than ahocorasick it is.
task_table <- function(task) {
  x <- comparison[comparison$task == task, ]
  ac <- x[x$method == "ahocorasick", c("case_id", "median_ms")]
  x$ratio <- x$median_ms / ac$median_ms[match(x$case_id, ac$case_id)]
  x$cell <- ifelse(
    x$method == "ahocorasick",
    fmt_ms(x$median_ms),
    paste0(fmt_ms(x$median_ms), " (", fmt_ratio(x$ratio), "×)")
  )
  out <- data.frame(Case = paste0("`", cases$case_id, "`"))
  for (method in names(method_labels)) {
    cells <- x$cell[x$method == method][match(cases$case_id, x$case_id[x$method == method])]
    out[[method_labels[[method]]]] <- ifelse(is.na(cells), "–", cells)
  }
  knitr::kable(out, align = c("l", rep("r", length(method_labels))))
}

# The range of "times slower than ahocorasick" for one method and task, over
# all cases it supports.
ratios <- function(task, method) {
  x <- comparison[comparison$task == task, ]
  ac <- x$median_ms[x$method == "ahocorasick"][
    match(x$case_id[x$method == method], x$case_id[x$method == "ahocorasick"])
  ]
  x$median_ms[x$method == method] / ac
}
ratio_range <- function(task, method) {
  r <- range(ratios(task, method))
  paste0(fmt_ratio(r[[1]]), "–", fmt_ratio(r[[2]]), "×")
}
# Cases where `ac_detect()` took less than a millisecond.
detect_ms <- comparison$median_ms[
  comparison$task == "detect" & comparison$method == "ahocorasick"
]
detect_fast <- paste(sum(detect_ms < 1), "of", length(detect_ms))

api_ms <- function(case_id, call) {
  fmt_ms(api$median_ms[api$case_id == case_id & api$call == call])
}
```

This article compares `ahocorasick` with other ways to search many fixed
strings in R, and then times each `ahocorasick` function. All numbers come from
one run on `r env[["date"]]`, on `r env[["cpu"]]` with `r env[["r_version"]]`.
They show relative costs on that machine; absolute times will differ on yours.

## What is compared

Every method answers three questions about each document:

- **detect**: does the document contain any of the patterns? Returns a logical
  vector.
- **count**: how many matches does it contain, counting overlapping matches?
  Returns an integer vector.
- **extract**: which matches does it contain, again with overlapping matches?
  Returns a data frame with one row per match and the document id.

Each method has to return these as R objects, so every timing includes turning
the result into something R code can use. The methods are:

| Method | How it searches |
| --- | --- |
| ahocorasick | `ac_detect()`, `ac_count(overlapping = TRUE)` and `ac_extract_df(overlapping = TRUE)`, with an automaton built before timing. `ac_extract_df()` also returns a `patterns` column, which the other methods do not. |
| Polars | `str$contains_any()`, `str$find_many()` and `str$extract_many()`, which also use the Rust aho-corasick crate. The timing includes creating a Polars DataFrame from the R character vector and converting the result back to R. |
| Polars (native) | The same expressions, on a DataFrame created before timing, and the results stay in Polars. This is the cost inside a Polars workflow. |
| AhoCorasickTrie | `AhoCorasickSearch()`. It builds its trie on every call, which is part of its timings, and it only supports ASCII, so it is skipped for Chinese and mixed text. |
| base R | A loop over the patterns, each searched in all documents at once with `grepl()` or `gregexpr()` and `fixed = TRUE`. `detect` stops searching a document once it matched. |
| stringr | The same loop with `str_detect()`, `str_count()` and `str_extract_all()` and `fixed()` patterns. |

Polars can use several threads; the other methods use one.

## Inputs

The documents are cut from three English novels (*Crime and Punishment*,
*Pride and Prejudice* and *The Count of Monte Cristo*) and four Chinese books
(`三体1-3`, `射雕英雄传`, `红楼梦` and `鲁迅全集`). English text is lowercased and
transliterated to ASCII. There are three document shapes:

- **medium**: 500 documents of 5,000 characters, taken evenly from all books.
  The mixed corpus joins half an English and half a Chinese document.
- **short**: 20,000 documents of 200 English or 100 Chinese characters.
- **long**: one document per book.

The patterns are the most frequent English words (`common` and `dict`), English
words of 7 or more letters that appear only a few times (`rare`), or the most
frequent runs of 2 to 4 Chinese characters.

```{r}
#| label: cases

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Case = paste0("`", cases$case_id, "`"),
    Documents = format(cases$docs_n, big.mark = ","),
    `Mean characters` = format(round(cases$mean_doc_chars), big.mark = ","),
    MiB = formatC(cases$input_mib, format = "f", digits = 2),
    Patterns = format(cases$patterns_n, big.mark = ","),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrrrr"
)
```

Patterns that can overlap themselves, such as "that", are left out. The base R
and stringr loops search one pattern at a time and never report such overlaps,
so their counts would differ from the Aho-Corasick methods.

## Correctness

Before timing, each method's result for every document is compared with the
base R result.
`r sum(correctness$status == "same")` results were identical to base R,
`r sum(correctness$status == "different")` differed, and
`r sum(correctness$status == "unsupported")` were skipped because the method
does not support the text.

## Results

Each table shows the median time in milliseconds, and in parentheses how many
times longer than `ahocorasick` it took. Each expression ran for at least
`r env[["min_time_seconds"]]` second and `r env[["min_iterations"]]`
iterations.

### Detect

```{r}
#| label: detect

task_table("detect")
```

The search in `ac_detect()` stops at the first match, so a good part of its
time is checking that every document is valid UTF-8, which reads the whole
text. It took less than a millisecond in `r detect_fast` cases; the
exceptions are the `rare` patterns, which few documents contain, so the whole
text is searched, and the 20,000 short Chinese documents. Polars
(native) does not check the text and took
`r ratio_range("detect", "polars_native")` the time of `ac_detect()`; from R,
converting the documents to Polars made it `r ratio_range("detect", "polars")`
as slow.

`detect` is the one task where a simple loop can be fastest. On the English,
mixed and long documents with the `common` and `dict` patterns, the first
pattern (`"the"` or `"一个"`) appears early in nearly every document, so the
base R and stringr loops finish after one or two patterns; on the medium
Chinese documents they were about as fast as `ac_detect()`. They lose this advantage when many
documents do not match the first patterns, as with the short Chinese
documents, and above all when few documents match at all, as with the `rare`
patterns, where they took
`r fmt_ms(comparison$median_ms[comparison$case_id == "en_medium_rare" & comparison$task == "detect" & comparison$method == "base"])`
ms against
`r fmt_ms(comparison$median_ms[comparison$case_id == "en_medium_rare" & comparison$task == "detect" & comparison$method == "ahocorasick"])`
ms for `ahocorasick`. AhoCorasickTrie builds its trie and finds every match
even to detect, so it was slow throughout.

### Count

```{r}
#| label: count

task_table("count")
```

`ahocorasick` and Polars (native) were close in every case, with Polars
(native) at `r ratio_range("count", "polars_native")` the time of
`ahocorasick`. Converting between R and Polars made Polars
`r ratio_range("count", "polars")` as slow. AhoCorasickTrie took
`r ratio_range("count", "AhoCorasickTrie")` as long, mostly because it rebuilds
its trie on every call. The base R and stringr loops scan every document once
per pattern, so they slow down with more patterns and with long documents:
`r ratio_range("count", "base")` and `r ratio_range("count", "stringr")` as
long as `ahocorasick`.

### Extract

```{r}
#| label: extract

task_table("extract")
```

Inside Polars, extracting took slightly longer than with `ahocorasick`
(`r ratio_range("extract", "polars_native")`). From R, Polars was
`r ratio_range("extract", "polars")` as slow, because turning its list column
of matches into an R data frame costs more than the search. The base R and
stringr loops took `r ratio_range("extract", "base")` and
`r ratio_range("extract", "stringr")` as long.

### Building the automaton

`ahocorasick` builds an automaton once and reuses it for every search.

```{r}
#| label: build

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    `Pattern set` = paste0("`", unique(build$pattern_set_id), "`"),
    Patterns = format(build$patterns_n[!duplicated(build$pattern_set_id)], big.mark = ","),
    `Median ms` = fmt_ms(build$median_ms[!duplicated(build$pattern_set_id)]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrr"
)
```

## `ahocorasick` functions

The median time in milliseconds of each search function, with the `common`
patterns. File functions search the same documents written to one file each,
and are not timed for short documents, which would need 20,000 files.

```{r}
#| label: api

api_cases <- unique(api$case_id)
api_table <- data.frame(Call = paste0("`", unique(api$call), "`"))
for (case_id in api_cases) {
  x <- api[api$case_id == case_id, ]
  api_table[[paste0("`", case_id, "`")]] <- fmt_ms(
    x$median_ms[match(unique(api$call), x$call)]
  )
}
knitr::kable(api_table, align = c("l", rep("r", length(api_cases))))
```

Functions that return one value per document (`ac_detect()`, `ac_count()`,
`ac_replace()`) cost little more than the search. Functions that return every
match cost more as matches grow, because each match becomes a row in R:
`ac_locate_df()` and `ac_extract_df()` return one data frame for all documents
and are faster than `ac_locate()` and `ac_extract()`, which return one data
frame per document. For example, with the short Chinese documents,
`ac_extract_df()` took `r api_ms("zh_short_common", "ac_extract_df()")` ms and
`ac_extract()` took `r api_ms("zh_short_common", "ac_extract()")` ms.

The file functions on `en_medium_common` open 500 files, and
`ac_replace_file()` also writes 500 files, which costs more than searching
5,000 characters in each.

## Summary

- For counting and extracting matches from R character vectors, `ahocorasick`
  was the fastest method in every case. Polars working on its own data
  counted about as fast and extracted slightly slower.
- For detecting, `ac_detect()` took less than a millisecond in `r detect_fast`
  cases. A loop over the patterns can be faster when common patterns match
  nearly every document, but is much slower when they do not.
- If your data already lives in a Polars DataFrame, Polars' `str$find_many()`
  and `str$extract_many()` are about as fast as `ahocorasick` and avoid
  converting data.
- The base R and stringr loops get slower with every added pattern, so they
  are only reasonable for a handful of patterns.

## Reproducing

The novels are in `bench/data/`. The first script cuts them into documents and
chooses the patterns; the second runs the comparison and writes the CSV files
in `bench/results/` that this article reads. Run them from the package root:

```{bash}
#| label: run-benchmarks
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

Rscript bench/01-generate-benchmark-data.R
Rscript bench/02-run-benchmarks.R
```

The second script needs the bench, Polars, AhoCorasickTrie.

```{r}
#| label: versions

pkgs <- grep("^package_", names(env), value = TRUE)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Package = sub("^package_", "", pkgs),
    Version = unname(env[pkgs])
  )
)
```
